items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A girl watering her tulsi plant and chewing a chapati at lunch opens the lesson: where does a plant's food come from, and where does ours go?

A leaf's inputs and outputs, a **starch test** and the **stomata** build photosynthesis; **Amoeba** shows the simplest way to take in food.

The meal is then followed juice by juice to the **villi** and the **large intestine**.

Several pictures are **animated**: let each one play while you narrate.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• plant cells, chloroplasts and the epidermis of a leaf

• osmosis: water moves into a cell from a weaker solution

• food contains carbohydrates, proteins and fats; iodine turns starch blue-black

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Write the photosynthesis equation and explain the roles of chlorophyll, stomata and guard cells.

**2.** Describe nutrition in Amoeba in one line.

**3.** Trace human digestion from mouth to large intestine, naming the main enzymes, juices and their actions.

**4.** Explain the role of villi in absorption.

**5.** Label diagrams of the human digestive system and a stoma.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Left: a girl **waters her tulsi plant** in the sunshine.

**Answer to Question 1**

Take guesses and leave it open. It **makes its own food** from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight (Part 1).

**What this shows**

Right: at lunch she **chews a chapati**; her plate also has dal and paneer.

**Answer to Question 2**

Take guesses and leave it open. **Saliva** turns starch into sugar (Part 3); food is broken into small molecules that pass into the blood in the **small intestine** (Part 4).

**What this shows**

**Step 1.** (a) A leaf with **green** and **white** parts, before the starch test.

**Answer to Question 3**

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: carbon dioxide gets in, and oxygen out, through the **stomata**. Then reveal the stoma (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1 only**

Reveal the labelled stoma: (a) open, (b) closed. Name the parts. **Do not click › yet**: the animation shows the answer to Question 4.

**Answer to Question 4**

**Step 3. Water.** When water flows into the guard cells they **swell** and curve apart, opening the pore; when they lose water they **shrink** and the pore closes. Then click › on the figure (pointer 4).

**Step 4: now click ›**

Picture 2: the guard cells **take in water and swell** (pore opens), then **lose water and shrink** (pore closes). Let it play two or three times, then click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop the movement.

*This picture is animated: it plays on its own and repeats.*

**Answer to Question 5**

**Step 5.** To **reduce water loss**; it closes them when it does not need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

**Step 6**

Read the key idea: the other raw material, **water**, comes through the **roots**, with minerals.

items.prompt: Name the parts labelled A, B and C in this stoma. Is it open or closed?
options: A guard cell, B stomatal pore, C chloroplast; open
A guard cell, B stomatal pore, C chloroplast; closed
A epidermal cell, B nucleus, C guard cell; open
A stomatal pore, B guard cell, C nucleus; closed

items.prompt: A plant is kept in a sealed glass jar with a chemical that absorbs all the carbon dioxide. After a few hours in sunlight, will its leaves contain starch?
options: Yes: sunlight is enough
No: carbon dioxide is a raw material
Yes: water is enough
No: oxygen is missing

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: A guard cell, B stomatal pore, C chloroplast (and D nucleus, E epidermal cell). **Open**: the guard cells are swollen and curved apart.

**On this question**

**No**: without carbon dioxide, a raw material, no glucose or starch can be made.

**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: **fungi** and **parasites**, and animals that take food in whole. Then ask Question 6 with the first picture.

**Answer to Question 6**

**Step 2: ask first**, with the still picture below as the reference. Take guesses, then reveal the figure and its animation (pointer 4). It pushes out temporary finger-like extensions (**pseudopodia**) that surround the food and fuse, trapping it in a **food vacuole**.

**What this shows**

**Step 1.** Two tubes of starch solution kept for 30 minutes, **A with saliva** and **B with water**, after a few drops of iodine.

**Answer to Question 8**

**Step 2.** Saliva contains the enzyme **salivary amylase**, which broke the starch in A into **sugar**; B still had starch. Chewed chapati tastes sweet for the same reason: Question 2 from the hook.

Read the key idea: the oesophagus pushes food down by **peristalsis**; then the **gastric juice** in the stomach. Then show peristalsis on the figure (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1, then click ›**

Picture 1: food entering the oesophagus. Click **›** to watch the muscles **squeeze behind the food**, pushing it down to the stomach. Click **‹** to return to picture 1.

**Answer to Question 9**

**Step 3.** The **HCl** makes the medium acidic so that pepsin can act, and kills germs. **Mucus** lines the stomach and protects it from the acid.

items.prompt: A person takes antacids so often that the stomach is hardly acidic any more. Which food will be digested poorly in the stomach?
options: Starch
Proteins
Fats
Vitamins

items.prompt: **Assertion (A):** Saliva begins the digestion of rice in the mouth. **Reason (R):** Salivary amylase breaks down starch into sugar.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
Both are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, R is false.
A is false, R is true.

items.text:
**On this question**

**Proteins**: pepsin needs the acidic medium made by HCl.

**On this question**

**(a)**: rice is mostly starch, which salivary amylase starts to break into sugar.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: digestion is completed in the **small intestine** by **three juices**. We take them one at a time.

**Answer to Question 10**

**Step 2.** It must be made **alkaline**. Then reveal the first juice (pointer 3).

**Step 3: reveal after Question 10**

Juice 1, **bile**, made by the liver: it makes the food alkaline and **emulsifies** fats.

**Step 4**

Read the key idea: bile is **not an enzyme**; it prepares the food for the pancreatic enzymes.

chunks.name: The small intestine: pancreatic and intestinal juice

items.text:
**Step 1**

Juice 2, **pancreatic juice**: three enzymes, one for each kind of food (amylase: starch; **trypsin**: proteins; **lipase**: fats).

**Step 2**

Juice 3, **intestinal juice**: its enzymes **complete** the digestion of all three.

**Step 3**

Read the key idea: the **end products** small enough to be absorbed.

items.text:
**What this shows**

**Step 1.** The inner wall of the small intestine, covered with **villi**, and one villus enlarged.

**Answer to Question 11**

**Step 2.** The villi give a **huge surface area** for absorption; the blood vessels take the absorbed food to every cell, where it is used for energy, growth and repair. Question 2 from the hook is now answered.

**Step 3**

Read the key idea: the **large intestine** absorbs water.

items.prompt: In this digestive system, which part makes bile, and in which part are the villi found?
options: D makes bile; villi line H
F makes bile; villi line I
G makes bile; villi line H
D makes bile; villi line I

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: bile is made by the liver, **D** (stored in F, the gall bladder); villi line the small intestine, **H**. All the parts: A mouth, B salivary glands, C oesophagus, D liver, E stomach, F gall bladder, G pancreas, H small intestine, I large intestine, J rectum, K anus.

items.prompt: A piece of paneer (protein) travels from the stomach to the blood. Which sequence of enzymes and end product is correct?
options: pepsin → trypsin → intestinal enzymes → amino acids
amylase → pepsin → lipase → glucose
pepsin → lipase → bile → fatty acids
trypsin → pepsin → amylase → amino acids

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: stomach, **pepsin**; small intestine, **trypsin**, then intestinal enzymes → **amino acids**, absorbed by the **villi** into the blood.
